title: Globalizing the professions
primary_topics: Globalization-of-professions doctrinal column April 6, 2014 -- second of three-part WTO-globalization arc (A420 Mar 30 → A419 Apr 6 → and forward)
Three-part vision-for-lawyers back-reference to A420 Mar 30 PBA speech: (1) ethical and competent (2) safeguard liberty and nurture prosperity (3) globalize their outlook and practice
Today's broader frame: globalization of ALL professions -- accounting, architecture, dentistry, engineering, medicine, nursing, etc.
WTO globalization of services framework: not only trade and industry (tariffs and taxes) but also services (free exchange of professions and blue-collar labor)
Filipino blue-collar globalization beneficiary: 10M Filipinos abroad, $26B remittances last year, Philippines economy 'second only to China' in growth pace
White-collar restrictions: Constitution limits practice to Filipino citizens 'save in cases prescribed by law'; by implication restricts Filipino professionals from foreign-practice reciprocity
RA 8981 reciprocity statute + Labor Code 'non-resident aliens' permits -- ~12,000 working permits issued in 2012

Asean 2015 integration single-market vision (goods + investments + capital + skilled labor + services); MRAs with Asean members -- engineering Dec 9 2005, nursing Dec 8 2006, architecture/land surveying Nov 19 2007, medicine/dentistry/accounting Feb 26 2009
Dean Andres D. Bautista (FEU Law) lecture -- one of 10 CJ Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity holders; four borderline-practice actual situations enumerated

Four borderline situations: (1) Architecture -- Shangri-La Fort Bonifacio 6-star hotel + Palmer & Turner SF/HK + Ove Arup + BTR/Davis Langdon/Seah quality surveyor + Recio & Casas local-sign; (2) Accountancy -- Del Monte Philippines Del Monte Foods US acquisition + Bill Bailey US-CPA via Isla Lipana-PWC; (3) Medicine -- Senator X stem-cell treatments Dr. G visits Manila quarterly for 10 friends at Edsa Shangri-La; (4) Law -- Hopewell Holdings HK $1.2B Sual Pangasinan power plant + Clifford Chance NY-HK lawyers travel to Manila for NY-law-governed loan documents
sub_topics: Other Sunday, CJP wrote on his vision for lawyers to (1) be ethical and competent (2) safeguard liberty and nurture prosperity (3) globalize their outlook and practice
Today, CJP will dwell on globalization of all professions: accounting, architecture, dentistry, engineering, medicine, nursing, etc.
World Trade Organization (WTO), of which Philippines is a member, has globalized not only trade and industry by breaking down tariffs and taxes that impede free flow of goods
But also services by encouraging free exchange of professions and blue-collar labor worldwide
Philippines is a major beneficiary of globalization of blue-collar labor
Over 10 million Filipinos employed abroad
Remitted $26 billion last year
Keeping Philippine economy bustling and growing at pace second only to China
On white-collar jobs (professions), story is a little different
Former Dean Andres D. Bautista of FEU Institute of Law and one of 10 holders of CJ Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity
Pointed out in recent lecture that Constitution limits practice of all professions to Filipino citizens 'save in cases prescribed by law'
By implication also restricts our professionals from practicing in foreign countries that demand reciprocity
Pursuant to constitutional exception, Congress enacted Republic Act No. 8981
Authorizing foreigners to practice here on reciprocal basis

I.e., laws of countries of foreign professionals 'allow citizens of the Philippines to practice the profession on the same basis and grant the same privileges as those enjoyed by citizens of such foreign states'

Labor Code allows 'non-resident aliens' to work here 'after a determination of non-availability of a person in the Philippines who is competent, able and willing at the time of the application to perform the services for which the alien is desired'
In 2012, about 12,000 working permits for foreigners were issued
Reciprocal exchange of professional practice urgently required by forthcoming integration of 10 member-countries (including Philippines) of Asean next year
Asean's 2015 vision is single market where goods, investments, capital, skilled labor and services freely flow
To prepare for integration, Dean Bautista reported Philippines entered into 'mutual recognition agreements' with Asean members for reciprocal professional practice by their citizens
Engineering -- Dec 9, 2005
Nursing -- Dec 8, 2006
Architecture and land surveying -- both Nov 19, 2007
Medicine, dentistry and accounting -- all Feb 26, 2009
Beyond Asean, Dean Bautista sketched some actual situations where borderline professional practice is already being done here
(1) Architecture: International hotel chain Shangri-La planning to build 6-star hotel in Fort Bonifacio
Engages Palmer & Turner -- foreign architectural firm based in San Francisco but with branch in Hong Kong
Also engaged structural engineer Ove Arup as design consultant
BTR Ltd., Davis Langdon and Seah as quality surveyor
Teams of foreign professionals visit project site on regular basis
Engages local architectural firm Recio & Casas to sign plans
After hotel is built, will employ several expatriates: general manager, hotel manager, resident manager, chef, etc.
(2) Accountancy: Del Monte Philippines looking to purchase Del Monte Foods operations of parent in United States
To complete purchase, needs accounting and audit advice in respect of Del Monte US' financial statements and condition
Bill Bailey, US CPA, works as consultant with Isla Lipana-PWC in Philippines
Del Monte Philippines would like to engage services of Mr. Bailey for purposes of providing advice on US accounting matters
(3) Medicine: Senator X has been traveling to Germany on regular basis to receive stem cell treatments in Dr. G's clinic
Seeing positive results in his physical demeanor, classmates have become envious
To help them and at same time save on costs, suggests to Dr. G that he visit Philippines and perform treatments on 10 of his friends
Latter book 10 rooms at Edsa Shangri-La
Share in travel and accommodation expenses of Dr. G in Manila
Dr. G now visits Manila every quarter to perform such services
(4) Law: Hong Kong-based energy developer Hopewell Holdings building $1.2-billion power plant in Sual, Pangasinan
Financing for project will be provided by consortium of export credit agencies such as IFC and Jexim and international commercial banks
Loan documents will be governed by New York law
HK developer engages services of international law firm Clifford Chance, with offices in New York and Hong Kong
Whose lawyers regularly travel to Manila to negotiate loan and security contracts
Questions: Are these foreigners (architects, accountants, doctors and lawyers) practicing their professions in the Philippines?
If so, are they practicing legally?
So asked 50-year-old Dean Bautista
Let us see what readers think of, and how they will react to, these real-life situations

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the second installment of his three-part WTO-globalization arc, broadening from lawyers (A420 March 30) to all professions. The other Sunday, CJ wrote on his vision for lawyers to (1) be ethical and competent, (2) safeguard the liberty and nurture the prosperity of our people, and (3) globalize their outlook and practice; today, CJ will dwell on the globalization of all professions: accounting, architecture, dentistry, engineering, medicine, nursing, etc. Globalization of services: the World Trade Organization (WTO), of which the Philippines is a member, has globalized not only trade and industry by breaking down tariffs and taxes that impede the free flow of goods, but also services by encouraging the free exchange of the professions and blue-collar labor worldwide. The Philippines is a major beneficiary of the globalization of blue-collar labor -- over 10 million Filipinos are employed abroad and remitted $26 billion last year, thus keeping the Philippine economy bustling and growing at a pace second only to China. On white-collar jobs (or professions), however, the story is a little different. Former Dean Andres D. Bautista of the Far Eastern University Institute of Law and one of 10 holders of the Chief Justice Panganiban Professorial Chairs on Liberty and Prosperity, pointed out in a recent lecture that our Constitution limits the practice of all professions to Filipino citizens, 'save in cases prescribed by law,' and by implication also restricts our professionals from practicing in foreign countries that demand reciprocity. Pursuant to the constitutional exception, Congress enacted RA 8981 authorizing foreigners to practice here on a reciprocal basis -- i.e., the laws of the countries of the foreign professionals 'allow citizens of the Philippines to practice the profession on the same basis and grant the same privileges as those enjoyed by citizens of such foreign states.' Also, our Labor Code allows 'non-resident aliens' to work here 'after a determination of non-availability of a person in the Philippines who is competent, able and willing at the time of the application to perform the services for which the alien is desired'; in 2012, about 12,000 working permits for foreigners were issued. Asean integration: the reciprocal exchange of professional practice is urgently required by the forthcoming integration of the 10 member-countries (including the Philippines) of Asean next year; Asean's 2015 vision is a single market where goods, investments, capital, skilled labor and services freely flow. To prepare for this integration, Dean Bautista reported that the Philippines entered into 'mutual recognition agreements' with Asean members for reciprocal professional practice by their citizens: engineering (Dec 9, 2005), nursing (Dec 8, 2006), architecture and land surveying (both Nov 19, 2007), and medicine, dentistry and accounting (all Feb 26, 2009). Borderline actual situations: beyond Asean, Dean Bautista sketched some actual situations where borderline professional practice is already being done here. (1) In architecture: 'International hotel chain Shangri-La is planning to build a 6-star hotel in Fort Bonifacio; it engages Palmer & Turner which is a foreign architectural firm based in San Francisco but with a branch in Hong Kong; it also engaged a structural engineer, Ove Arup, as design consultant, BTR Ltd., Davis Langdon and Seah as quality surveyor; teams of foreign professionals visit the project site on a regular basis; it engages a local architectural firm, Recio & Casas, to sign the plans; after the hotel is built, it will be employing several expatriates: general manager, hotel manager, resident manager, chef, etc.' (2) In accountancy: 'Del Monte Philippines is looking to purchase the Del Monte Foods operations of its parent in the US; to complete the purchase, it needs accounting and audit advice in respect of Del Monte US' financial statements and condition; Bill Bailey, a US CPA, works as a consultant with Isla Lipana-PWC in the Philippines; Del Monte Philippines would like to engage the services of Mr. Bailey for purposes of providing advice on US accounting matters.' (3) In medicine: 'Senator X has been traveling to Germany on a regular basis to receive stem cell treatments in Dr. G's clinic; seeing the positive results in his physical demeanor, his classmates have become envious of him; to help them and at the same time save on costs, he suggests to Dr. G that he visit the Philippines and perform the treatments on 10 of his friends; the latter book 10 rooms at Edsa Shangri-La; they also share in the travel and accommodation expenses of Dr. G in Manila; Dr. G now visits Manila every quarter to perform such services.' (4) In law: 'Hong Kong-based energy developer Hopewell Holdings is building a $1.2-billion power plant in Sual, Pangasinan; financing for the project will be provided by a consortium of export credit agencies such as the IFC and Jexim and international commercial banks; the loan documents will be governed by New York law; the HK developer engages the services of an international law firm, Clifford Chance, with offices in New York and Hong Kong whose lawyers regularly travel to Manila to negotiate the loan and security contracts.' Questions: are these foreigners (architects, accountants, doctors and lawyers) practicing their professions in the Philippines? If so, are they practicing legally? So asked 50-year-old Dean Bautista; let us see what readers think of, and how they will react to, these real-life situations.
